Reproducibility

How the fictional data were generated

A fixed-seed generator draws fictional lodging prices and group attributes, then creates separate probability and firm-association examples. The appendix identifies which mechanism belongs to each case.

Fixed seed: 42022. Read the complete generator and analysis code; inspect the saved results.

Known truth: The case draws towns with different price distributions. The overall mean therefore changes with the mix of destinations, while town-level coverage shows where the cap will be hardest to use.

These are model assumptions and generated outcomes, not claims about a real population.

Stop 01 / 24

Read one observation before reading the distribution

This lesson generates 360 independent fictional lodging quotes from explicitly chosen lognormal models. Willow Bay contributes 180, Cedar Reach 110 and Juniper Vale 70. Each row is one quoted nightly price in fictional CU under a common assumed room specification. These are new observations, separate from Lesson 1’s preparation example.

A distribution describes which values occur and how frequently. Start with support, units, missingness and the observation definition before interpreting shape. A high price may be legitimate, a unit error or a different product. A histogram alone cannot distinguish these explanations.

  • Observed range: 50.95 to 272.94 CU.
  • Target here: the generated quote population under the stated mechanism.
  • Not observed: actual availability, guest experiences, purchases or real-market prices.

Pause and explain

What does one price observation say about what a customer paid?

Compare your reasoning

Only what was quoted in this synthetic case. A quote is not an accepted booking or a realized payment.

Stop 02 / 24

Count, proportion and density use different scales

A count is the number of observations in a bin. A proportion divides that count by the sample size. A density also divides by bin width, so probability is represented by rectangle area. This matters when widths differ: a wider bin can contain more observations simply because it covers a larger interval.

Bin density = count / (sample size × bin width); bin probability = density × width
Unequal-width density histogram of synthetic nightly prices — chart data
BinProbability per CU
[0, 80)0.001424
[80, 120)0.009861
[120, 180)0.006528
[180, 300]0.000833

The areas sum to one over the displayed full range. Heights do not. The final interval includes its upper endpoint; other intervals include the lower endpoint and exclude the upper. With continuous measurements, boundary conventions rarely change much, but the implementation still needs one.

Pause and explain

A width-40 bin has density 0.005 per CU. What share does it contain?

Compare your reasoning

Its area is 40 × 0.005 = 0.20, or 20%. Density has inverse-price units; it is not itself a probability at a point.

Stop 03 / 24

Change bins and look for stable features

Bin width is an analytical choice, not a feature of the underlying observations. Very narrow bins show noisy local fluctuations; very wide bins can hide modes or gaps. Shift the origin or change width and ask which conclusions survive. Keep the observations and denominator fixed while changing the view.

Pause and explain

If one binning looks bimodal and another does not, what should you report?

Compare your reasoning

The apparent second mode is sensitive to bin choices. Inspect finer evidence and the collection process rather than presenting one histogram as conclusive.

Stop 04 / 24

Name the denominator before comparing a percentage

A percentage is incomplete without the event and the population. “Under budget” here means price ≤ 140 CU, among all generated quotes in the relevant town. A percentage among hotels, among complete quotes or among refundable offers can differ because each uses a different denominator.

Synthetic budget shares with denominators
Fictional townQuotesAt most 140 CUWithin-town share
Willow Bay18015787.2%
Cedar Reach1105348.2%
Juniper Vale705274.3%

Raw counts can make a large group look better even when its share is lower. A location filter changes the target population, so document it before recomputing the percentage. A histogram cropped to central values also needs disclosure: if counts outside the view disappear, readers may mistake a conditional distribution for the full one.

Pause and explain

Can 60 affordable quotes out of 100 be compared with 80 out of 200 using counts alone?

Compare your reasoning

Not to compare affordability rates. The shares are 60% and 40%. Counts answer inventory volume; shares answer the within-group frequency.

Stop 05 / 24

Mean, median and mode answer different questions

The overall synthetic mean is 123.73 CU and the median is 119.08 CU. The mean uses every value and is relevant to expected total spending under random sampling from this mix. The median splits observations into halves and describes a typical central quote. A mode identifies a most frequent value or region, but continuous-price modes depend on rounding, bins or smoothing.

Synthetic sensitivity of mean and median
Toy datasetValuesMeanMedian
Original50, 60, 70, 80, 9070.0070.00
One changed value50, 60, 70, 80, 250102.0070.00

The mean moves sharply when one large value changes because its contribution is linear in the total. The median does not move here because the middle order statistic is unchanged. Robustness is useful, but neither summary is universally superior: choose the statistic that matches the decision.

Pause and explain

Which summary is more directly connected to the total cost of many randomly selected stays?

Compare your reasoning

The mean, multiplied by the number of stays, under a stable and relevant sampling mix. The median is not generally additive.

Stop 06 / 24

Use quantiles and deviations to describe variability

The first quartile is 97.64 CU, the third quartile is 142.31 CU and the interquartile range is 44.67 CU. The sample SD is 40.20 CU. Quantiles locate positions in the ordered sample; SD describes squared deviations around the mean. They answer different questions and react differently to extremes.

Sample variance s² = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² / (n − 1); sample SD s = √s²

The n − 1 denominator makes sample variance unbiased for population variance under IID sampling with finite variance. It does not make SD itself exactly unbiased. Squaring deviations gives distant observations more influence. The IQR is resistant to a small number of extremes but omits tail magnitude.

The lab uses NumPy’s linear-interpolation quantiles. A quartile can fall between observed prices; it need not be a price actually quoted. Different documented quantile conventions can produce small differences, especially in tiny samples.

Pause and explain

If all prices are multiplied by 1.1, what happens to variance and SD?

Compare your reasoning

SD is multiplied by 1.1, while variance is multiplied by 1.1² = 1.21. Both the location and units must be considered when comparing variability.

Stop 07 / 24

Describe shape, then investigate unusual values

The generated price distribution is right-skewed, with sample skewness 0.995. Its Tukey fences are 30.63 and 209.32 CU. There are 15 observations beyond those fences. These are screening flags, not proof of error.

Five-number boxplot components using Tukey whiskers
FeatureSynthetic value
Lower whisker50.95
Q197.64
Median119.08
Q3142.31
Upper whisker208.06

Whiskers extend to the most extreme observed values still within the fences, not automatically to the fence values themselves. The range records the full observed extremes. Investigate unusual records in their original context: currency conversion, room mix, premium products and data-entry errors can produce similar visual signals.

Deleting observations because they make the result inconvenient changes the estimand. If an exclusion is justified, state the rule, its reason and a sensitivity comparison retaining the flagged records.

Pause and explain

Is an observation beyond Q3 + 1.5 × IQR necessarily invalid?

Compare your reasoning

No. The rule identifies unusual values relative to the sample’s central spread. A legitimate premium offer may belong in the population.

Stop 08 / 24

A smooth curve adds assumptions

A kernel density estimate places a small smooth bump around each observed value and averages the bumps. Its bandwidth controls smoothing: a small bandwidth can chase noise; a large one can erase structure. A violin plot mirrors a smoothed density, so its width is not a direct count of observations.

The lab’s Gaussian KDE uses its default Scott bandwidth, corresponding to a kernel SD of 12.39 CU. The displayed grid is only a sampled curve, not the calculation used for exact event shares. Gaussian kernels can assign density below zero, which is outside the support of prices. A log-scale model or boundary correction may be more appropriate near a hard boundary.

Pause and explain

Does a violin with the same displayed width mean two groups have the same number of rows?

Compare your reasoning

Not generally. Many plotting tools normalize each group’s density separately. Show sample sizes and state the width convention.

Stop 09 / 24

Attach group labels without duplicating observations

Before comparing towns or refund policies, attach attributes at the correct level. If several price observations belong to one lodging, a lodging dimension should have one row per lodging. A many-to-one join is appropriate only if the attribute is stable across the quoted dates; otherwise the key also needs time.

The current lab generates each quote with its group label directly, so no external join is needed. In an operational workflow, validate the dimension key, check unmatched rows and compare counts before and after joining. A duplicate feature record would give some prices extra weight and distort both the distribution and the group mean.

  • Verify common currency, stay length and room specification.
  • Hold the time window and eligibility rules constant.
  • Report missing attribute matches rather than silently dropping them.
  • Retain row IDs so an apparent group difference can be traced back to observations.

Pause and explain

A duplicate feature row only repeats information. Why can it still change the result?

Compare your reasoning

The join repeats the associated price observations too, increasing their statistical weight. Repeated values are not harmless if later counts and averages include them.

Stop 10 / 24

Compare unequal groups on a common basis

Use common axes and common definitions. Count histograms answer how many observations occur; normalized histograms answer where a group’s probability mass lies. Equal visual area can make unequal-size groups easier to compare, but the sample size must remain visible. Otherwise the more uncertain small group can appear equally well supported.

A mean difference can arise from group composition rather than a uniform shift affecting every offer. Compare central spread and tails as well as centers. None of these descriptive summaries includes sampling uncertainty yet; Lesson 3 adds that layer.

Pause and explain

Why keep the same price axis for every town?

Compare your reasoning

Changing axes can exaggerate or conceal differences. Common units, limits and bin definitions make visual comparisons interpretable.

Stop 11 / 24

Turn a distribution into a bounded budget statement

A budget needs a tolerance for overruns, not just a central value. Ask whether the decision is about expected spending, the share under a cap, or a high quantile that protects against expensive cases. These lead to different summaries. A mean can sit below a cap while many individual quotes exceed it.

Across this synthetic mix, 72.8% of quotes are at most 140 CU. The overall median is 119.08 CU, and the middle half spans 97.64–142.31 CU. Those numbers describe the generated mix; they are not a guarantee about the next real trip.

  • For expected total cost: use a relevant mean and state the volume assumption.
  • For a booking cap: report the event definition and the within-group share.
  • For unusually costly cases: inspect upper quantiles and the process generating the tail.
  • For a recommendation: state which costs and constraints remain unmeasured.

Pause and explain

What is missing from “the average is below budget, so the budget is sufficient”?

Compare your reasoning

The variability, probability of exceeding the cap, relevant population mix and the decision-maker’s tolerance for an overrun.

Stop 12 / 24

A probability needs a defined event and sample space

An empirical proportion describes observed rows. A probability model describes possible outcomes under assumptions. They connect through sampling, but they are not interchangeable. Define A = quote ≤ 140 CU and R = refundable. The table below is the full synthetic sample space for these two binary events.

Synthetic event counts
Refund termsA: ≤140 CUNot A: >140 CUTotal
Refundable15965224
Not refundable10333136
Total26298360
P(A ∪ R) = P(A) + P(R) − P(A ∩ R)

Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together. Independent events satisfy P(A ∩ R) = P(A)P(R). Nontrivial mutually exclusive events are not independent: learning that one occurred rules out the other. For a continuous model, probability at one exact point is zero even when its density is high.

Pause and explain

Are “refundable” and “at most 140 CU” mutually exclusive?

Compare your reasoning

No. Their intersection contains 159 generated quotes. A row can have both properties.

Stop 13 / 24

Conditioning changes the denominator; Bayes reverses it

Among refundable offers, 71.0% cost at most 140 CU. Among offers at most 140 CU, 60.7% are refundable. These are different conditional probabilities because they condition on different groups.

P(A | R) = P(A ∩ R) / P(R); P(R | A) = P(A | R)P(R) / P(A)

For the first probability the denominator is 224; for the reverse it is 262. Bayes’ rule connects them through the base rates. The same conditioning logic applies to means: the average refundable quote is 124.13 CU, compared with 123.07 CU among nonrefundable quotes.

The generator makes refund status independent of price within every town. Finite samples will still show accidental differences. An observed conditional difference is not automatically proof that the population probabilities differ, and neither conditional probability alone describes a causal effect of refund terms.

Pause and explain

If P(A | R) is high, must P(R | A) also be high?

Compare your reasoning

No. The reverse probability also depends on how common refundable offers are. Confusing the two drops the base-rate information.

Stop 14 / 24

Expected value is a probability-weighted average

A separate authored service-reward model has three possible net rewards. Unlike the quote sample, these probabilities are stipulated, not estimated. Multiply each reward by its probability and sum. An expected value can lie between outcomes and need not be possible in any single trial.

Synthetic service-reward model
Net reward CUProbabilityContribution to E[X]
-4.00.55-2.20
6.00.31.80
18.00.152.70
E[X] = Σ x p(x) = 2.30 CU; Var(X) = E[(X − E[X])²] = 62.91 CU²

The SD is 7.93 CU. For n independent repetitions, the expected total is nE[X] and its variance is nVar(X). Expected values add even without independence, but variances then need covariance terms. A favorable expectation does not eliminate loss risk, cash-flow constraints or dislike of volatility.

Pause and explain

Could the model’s expected reward be received in a single trial?

Compare your reasoning

Not here: 2.30 CU is not one of the three outcomes. It is a long-run probability-weighted average under the model.

Stop 15 / 24

Choose a distribution from the mechanism and support

A distribution family is a claim about a process. A binomial model counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials with one success probability. A Poisson model counts events over exposure under a stable rate and appropriate independence. A normal model describes an unbounded continuous quantity; an exponential model describes nonnegative waiting times under a constant hazard.

The binomial bars are probability masses at integers, not a continuous density. Check support before shape: a normal approximation can assign impossible negative counts or prices. Dependence and changing rates can invalidate a family even when a histogram looks plausible.

Pause and explain

Would a binomial model automatically fit repeated outcomes from the same customer?

Compare your reasoning

No. Repeated behavior can be dependent, and customers can have different success probabilities. The mechanism needs examination before using the formula.

Stop 16 / 24

Positive skew and tail risk need separate attention

A lognormal variable is the exponential of a normal variable. It is positive and right-skewed. Multiplicative variation makes it a useful teaching model for prices and sizes, but shape alone does not establish that it is correct. Its mean is larger than its median when the log variance is positive.

If log X ~ Normal(4.7, 0.4²), median(X) = exp(4.7) = 109.95; E[X] = exp(4.7 + 0.4²/2) = 119.10

A Pareto model with minimum 50 and shape α = 1.5 has mean 150.00 and P(X > 200) = 0.1250. Its variance is infinite. A Pareto mean exists only for α > 1; its variance exists only for α > 2. Thus the usual finite-variance CLT and familiar standard-error formulas do not automatically apply.

Large extremes can dominate averages even when the central histogram appears stable. Investigate tail mechanisms, aggregation and top-coding. Do not fit a tail model merely to obtain a dramatic story, and do not apply “normal because n is large” without checking the assumptions relevant to the estimator.

Pause and explain

Does a finite sample SD prove the population variance is finite?

Compare your reasoning

No. Every finite dataset can have a finite calculated SD even when the assumed population model has infinite variance.

Stop 17 / 24

Introduce a new case without switching indicators silently

We now move to 240 fictional firms. Each row has a noisy practice score between 1 and 5, a simulated employee count and a sector label. A latent trait influences both score and size, while independent noise and sector composition add variation. Those assumptions deliberately create association; they are not evidence from real firms.

The practice score is a proxy, not the latent concept itself. Measurement error can attenuate or otherwise distort associations. Employee count measures scale, not profit, productivity or performance. Renaming it “success” would make an unsupported conceptual substitution.

Pause and explain

Does a practice score directly measure the quality of every management decision?

Compare your reasoning

No. It is a noisy, limited proxy. Interpretation must stay with what the score actually captures and acknowledge the measurement process.

Stop 18 / 24

Compare each group on its own denominator

Define a “large firm” as employee count ≥ 60, then calculate the share within each score band. The band boundaries are lower: score < 2.5; middle: 2.5 ≤ score < 3.5; higher: score ≥ 3.5. A threshold is a chosen definition, not a natural law.

Pause and explain

What changes if “large” is redefined from 60 to 80 employees?

Compare your reasoning

The event changes, so its counts and probabilities must be recalculated. The old percentages no longer answer the new question.

Stop 19 / 24

Group averages can hide overlap and composition

A higher group mean does not mean every observation in that group exceeds every observation in another. It can coexist with substantial overlap. A pooled association can even reverse within strata if groups have different compositions. The authored counts below make that reversal visible without relying on a real-world dataset.

Synthetic composition example

Training has the higher share within both sectors. Pooled across sectors, Training is 42.0% and Comparison is 74.0%. Training contains many more difficult-sector cases. The pooled groups do not compare the same mix.

This is a descriptive warning, not a rule that every adjustment is correct. The decision and causal structure determine which variables should be conditioned on. Automatically controlling for every available variable can introduce other biases.

Pause and explain

Do these counts prove training causes improvement?

Compare your reasoning

No. They illustrate composition reversal. Causal interpretation also requires a defensible assignment mechanism and appropriate adjustment choices.

Stop 20 / 24

A binned mean is not an individual firm

Divide score into ten equal-count groups and plot the mean score against mean employee count in each group. This binned scatter clarifies the average pattern but hides within-bin variation and can make a noisy individual relationship look tight. Equal-count groups need not have equal score widths.

Report the binning rule and do not calculate an individual-level correlation from the ten averages as if they were the original observations.

Pause and explain

Why might the correlation of binned averages be larger than the individual correlation?

Compare your reasoning

Averaging suppresses within-bin noise. The resulting coefficient describes an aggregated relationship, not the precision of predictions for individual firms.

Stop 21 / 24

Keep paired deviations together

Covariance asks whether observations above their own variable’s mean also tend to be above the other variable’s mean. Keep the original pairs: separately sorting the two columns creates a different relationship. Positive products contribute positive covariance, while opposite-signed deviations contribute negative covariance.

Sample covariance sₓᵧ = Σ[(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ)] / (n − 1)

The three-pair example has covariance 1.50. In the firm sample, covariance is 13.54 score-unit × employees. Covariance changes if either variable’s scale changes, so its magnitude is difficult to compare across differently measured relationships.

Pause and explain

What would happen if you sorted the employee column but left scores in their original order?

Compare your reasoning

You would destroy the original pairing and calculate an association for fabricated pairs. The rows, not the separate marginal distributions, define covariance.

Stop 22 / 24

Correlation removes units, not complexity

Pearson correlation is covariance divided by the product of sample SDs. The synthetic score–employee correlation is 0.422. Using log employee count changes it to 0.450 because a nonlinear transformation changes the relationship being summarized. Positive rescaling alone would not change correlation.

This symmetric U-shaped example has r = 0.000, up to floating-point rounding, despite a deterministic relationship. Zero correlation rules out neither dependence nor useful prediction. Pearson r describes linear association and can be sensitive to extreme points and restricted ranges. A correlation matrix still needs scatterplots, sample sizes and missing-data rules.

Pause and explain

If two variables have correlation zero, can one help predict the other?

Compare your reasoning

Yes. Here y = x² predicts y exactly, while the positive and negative linear contributions cancel.

Stop 23 / 24

Description, prediction and intervention are different tasks

Description summarizes the observed joint distribution. Prediction uses available features to forecast outcomes in new observations and requires out-of-sample validation. Causal inference asks what would change if an intervention altered one factor while the relevant alternatives were held appropriately comparable.

The firm generator includes a common latent cause of score and size. Therefore an association is built in even though the script specifies no causal arrow from the measured score to employee count. The simulation exposes a general risk: raising a reported score does not necessarily change the underlying process.

  • Confounding: another factor influences both variables.
  • Reverse direction: size can influence resources available for practices.
  • Selection: the observed firms differ from the population of interest.
  • Measurement: scores and scale measures imperfectly represent the intended concepts.

A large coefficient can also be operationally unimportant, while a modest association may be useful for a specific forecast. Evaluate the decision, cost of errors and stability across populations rather than ranking importance by correlation alone.

Pause and explain

What additional evidence would support a claim about changing management practice?

Compare your reasoning

A credible intervention or quasi-experimental design, clear treatment and outcome definitions, defensible assumptions and a relevant target population. Correlation alone is insufficient.

Stop 24 / 24

Deliver a distribution-aware decision brief

A useful brief starts with the population and observation, then reports a small set of summaries selected for the decision. Name the event and denominator for every percentage. Show at least one view of shape and one view of variation. Distinguish an observed frequency from a stipulated probability model.

A reusable Lesson 2 handoff structure
Claim typeWhat to include
Budget descriptionPrice definition, mean/median, spread, cap share and n
Group comparisonCommon scope, within-group denominators and composition
Probability modelSupport, mechanism, parameters and calculated event
AssociationPaired unit, scatterplot, coefficient and noncausal limitation

Example: “In 360 simulated quotes, 72.8% are at most 140 CU. The median is 119.08 CU, with a right tail and meaningful town differences. These results describe the authored scenario, not current hotel prices. For a real budget, validate the market frame and quantify uncertainty.”

Next, Lesson 3 separates variation among observations from uncertainty in an estimate, and asks which population claims a sampling design can support.

Pause and explain

What should you avoid adding to this descriptive brief?

Compare your reasoning

A causal explanation, a population certainty claim or a real-market recommendation that the synthetic design and analysis do not support.
